events.text: Your mother, {npc}, drags a camphor-wood box out from under the bed. Inside is everything you ever drew, scribbled or folded as a child: a horse with six legs, a letter to the moon, a paper boat. 'Help me sort it,' {he} says. 'I cannot throw any of it away, so we will just sort it.'

choices.text: Sort it all, slowly, and laugh at every one

mem.note: sorted the scrap box with me

effects.log: It takes the whole afternoon. The letter to the moon says the moon should come down for dinner. {npc} reads it aloud twice.

choices.text: Draw {npc} a new horse with the right number of legs

effects.log: Four legs, finally. {npc} puts it on top of the six-legged one and says it is not as good.

events.text: {npc} has kept every letter you sent home, too, in the same box, under the six-legged horse. {He} wants you to read one aloud, the one from your first year away, because {he} cannot read your handwriting.

choices.text: Read it aloud, every brave lie in it

effects.log: You wrote that you were eating well and sleeping well and not cold at all. {npc} listens and says, 'I knew you were cold.'

choices.text: Write a new letter, sitting right beside {npc}

effects.log: You write it while {npc} watches: the truth this time. {He} folds it and puts it in the box on top of everything.

events.text: {npc} hands you the camphor-wood box to keep. 'It is yours,' {he} says. 'It always was. I was only minding it.'

choices.text: Keep it under your own bed

effects.log: It goes under your bed. Some nights you open it and look at the six-legged horse, and the house feels full.

choices.text: Add something of {npc}'s to it before taking it

mem.note: asked for something of mine for the box

effects.log: You ask {npc} for one thing: a hair ribbon, a recipe, a few lines. {He} writes three lines and will not let you read them until later. You do not open them yet.

events.text: Your mother, {npc}, is at war. The neighbour's goose eats {his} cabbages every night, and the neighbour denies everything. {npc} wants your help, and has a stick.

choices.text: Build a better fence

effects.log: Bamboo, twine and a whole Sunday. The goose stands outside it the next morning, staring at you with deep contempt. The cabbages live.

choices.text: Go and talk to the neighbour

effects.log: The neighbour is very old and the goose is the neighbour's only company. You come back with a peace offer: one cabbage a week, for the goose, given freely.

events.text: The goose war has entered a new phase. The goose has learned to open the gate. {npc} has learned to throw shoes. The neighbour has started throwing shoes back.

choices.text: Train the goose

effects.log: It takes a month of bread crusts and patience. The goose follows you around the lane like a dog, and leaves the cabbages alone. {npc} is horrified and impressed.

choices.text: Invite the neighbour to dinner, goose included

effects.log: Cabbage soup. The neighbour and {npc} argue about cabbages all evening and enjoy it. The goose sits on the step and is given scraps.

events.text: The goose is very old now, and so is the neighbour. You find {npc} out in the garden at dusk, quietly putting a cabbage over the fence.

choices.text: Pretend not to see

mem.note: pretended not to see the cabbage

effects.log: You go back inside. Some wars end better than others. This one ends with a cabbage over a fence every evening.

choices.text: Help {npc} carry two

mem.note: carried cabbages over the fence with me

effects.log: You carry two cabbages over the fence together. The goose honks, once, very feebly. {npc} honks back.

events.text: Your mother, {npc}, never learned {his} letters; there was never time. Tonight {he} puts a brush and a sheet of paper in front of you and says, very fast, as if it does not matter: 'Teach me to write my own name.'

choices.text: Teach {npc} to write the name

effects.log: Seven strokes, then nine. {npc}'s hand shakes. On the twentieth try the name stands on the page, crooked and whole. {npc} looks at it for a long time.

choices.text: Teach {npc} your name first

mem.note: taught me to write their name

effects.log: {npc} writes your name before {his} own. It is the first word {npc} ever writes. You both pretend that is a normal thing to cry about.

events.text: {npc} has been practising. There are sheets of characters all over the kitchen, some on the pickle jars. Now {he} wants to learn enough to write you a letter.

choices.text: Teach {npc} a hundred characters

effects.log: Rice, river, rain, home, cold, come back. {npc} learns them all in a season, the way {he} once learned to bargain at the market: fiercely.

choices.text: Make {npc} a book of the characters to keep

mem.note: made me a book of characters

effects.log: You write each one large with a little drawing. {npc} keeps it by the stove and studies it while the rice cooks.

events.text: A letter arrives for you. The characters are huge and wobbly, and some are wrong. It is from {npc}. It says that the rice is cooking, the river is high, it is cold, and come back.

choices.text: Come back at once

effects.log: You walk two days. {npc} is at the stove when you arrive, and points at the letter in your hand and says, 'I wrote that.'

choices.text: Write back, in characters {npc} knows

effects.log: Rice, river, rain, home. You use only the hundred. The answer comes back a month later with two new characters in it that you never taught.

events.text: Your mother, {npc}, is going to market, and wants you to come and carry. Everyone at the market knows {npc}. Stallholders hide the good fish when {he} comes.

choices.text: Carry, and watch {npc} bargain

effects.log: {npc} gets a fish, a cabbage and three eggs for the price of the fish. The fish seller looks like someone who has been robbed politely.

choices.text: Try bargaining for the eggs yourself

effects.log: You get the eggs at full price and a free sympathy egg. {npc} says that is a start, and that the sympathy egg was the real victory.

events.text: Market day again. This time {npc} hands you the money and the basket. 'Bring back everything on the list and half the silver,' {he} says. 'I will be at the tea stall, watching.'

choices.text: Bargain like {npc}

ok.log: Everything on the list, and half the silver back, and a free bunch of spring onions out of respect. {npc} nods at the tea stall like a general.

fail.log: Everything on the list, and no silver back at all. {npc} takes the basket and goes back down the market and recovers half the silver in a quarter of an hour.

choices.text: Pay full price and be loved by every stall

effects.log: You are the most popular person at the market. {npc} is ashamed of you, and secretly a little proud.

events.text: {npc}'s knees will not take the market any more. {He} gives you the list, the basket and the silver, and a stern look. 'They will try to rob you because they miss me.'

choices.text: Go and bargain in {npc}'s name

effects.log: Every stallholder asks after {npc}. The fish seller sends a fish, free, with a message: tell {npc} the market is too quiet. {npc} is delighted.

choices.text: Carry {npc} to the market in a borrowed cart

effects.log: {npc} sits in the cart like an empress and bargains from it. The stalls fall like a walled city. It is the best day the market has had in years.

events.arc: The Herb from Over the Pass
events.text: Your mother, {npc}, has a winter cough that will not lift, and says the only thing that ever helped was a herb from an old physician over the pass. {He} asks if you would go, and then tells you not to, in the same breath.

choices.text: Go over the pass in the snow

mem.note: crossed the pass for my cough

ok.log: Three days, cold to the bone. The old physician gives you the herb and refuses money. {npc} drinks the tea and the cough lifts within the week.

mem.note: caught my cough fetching the herb

fail.log: You lose the path for a day and come back with the herb and a cough of your own. {npc} nurses you both with the same pot of tea.

choices.text: Send a porter with silver (12 taels)

effects.log: The porter brings back the herb and a letter from the old physician with instructions in large characters. {npc} follows them exactly and the cough goes.

events.arc: The Herb from Over the Pass
events.text: {npc} has decided the herb should not have to come over the pass. {He} wants to grow it in the garden, and has bought seeds from a pedlar who was probably lying.

choices.text: Dig a shady bed by the north wall

effects.log: The pedlar was lying about half the seeds. The other half come up, thin and real. {npc} talks to them every morning.

choices.text: Write to the old physician for proper seeds

effects.log: A packet comes back with the seeds and a sketch of the plant. {npc} frames the sketch.

events.arc: The Herb from Over the Pass
events.text: The north wall is green with the herb now. Half the lane comes to {npc} for it in winter, and {npc} makes them sit and drink it in the kitchen and tell {him} all their news.

choices.text: Help {npc} dry a winter's worth

effects.log: Bundles hang from every beam. The house smells of the pass in winter. {npc} says that is how it should smell.

choices.text: Take a bundle back over the pass to the physician

mem.note: took my herb back over the pass

effects.log: The old physician laughs to see it come back the other way, and gives you a cup of tea from it.

events.text: Your father, {npc}, has been building a boat in the shed for six years. It is nearly finished, {he} says, as {he} has said for five of them. Today {he} asks you to hold a plank.

choices.text: Hold the plank, and then another

effects.log: You hold planks all afternoon. {npc} talks to the boat more than to you, and you realise that is how {he} says things.

choices.text: Ask when it will be finished

mem.note: chose the colour of the prow

effects.log: {npc} looks at the boat for a long time. 'When it is right,' {he} says. Then {he} lets you choose the colour of the prow.

events.text: The boat is finished. {npc} wants to launch it on the river at dawn, with nobody watching except you, in case it sinks.

choices.text: Launch it together

ok.log: It floats. It floats very well. {npc} sits in it in the middle of the river and does not say anything for an hour, and neither do you.

fail.log: It floats, then lists, then gently fills. You both swim back pushing it. {npc} laughs harder than you have ever heard. 'Six more years,' {he} says.

choices.text: Name it before it touches the water

effects.log: You paint a name on the prow. {npc} reads it and has to go back into the shed for a moment.

events.text: {npc} takes the boat out less now. This morning {he} is at your door before dawn with two fishing rods and the look of someone who has something to say and will not say it on land.

choices.text: Go out on the river with {npc}

effects.log: You fish all morning. Out in the middle, {npc} says the thing, finally, the thing about the years when you did not speak. Then {he} catches a carp, and you both shout.

choices.text: Row, and let {npc} fish

effects.log: You row. {npc} fishes, and says nothing, and that is the thing, too. The boat is dry the whole way.

events.text: Your father, {npc}, borrowed silver from you last year for seed, and has not mentioned it since. Today {he} arrives with a handcart full of pickled radishes. 'Interest,' {he} says. 'The silver is coming.'

choices.text: Accept the radishes with great ceremony

effects.log: You stack eighty jars of radish in the kitchen. The silver arrives in the autumn, every copper. You eat radishes until spring.

choices.text: Say the radishes cover the whole debt

effects.log: {npc} is offended, then relieved, then offended again. You eat radishes until spring, and {npc} brings more anyway.

events.text: The radishes have got famous. People in the lane trade for {npc}'s pickled radish now, and {he} wants to sell them at the market, with a sign. {He} wants your help with the sign.

choices.text: Paint a grand sign

effects.log: You paint: The Radish of the Year. {npc} says it is shameless and hangs it up at once.

choices.text: Help {npc} carry the jars to market

effects.log: The first market day sells half the jars. {npc} counts the coins three times and gives you some, as interest.

events.text: {npc}'s radish stall has a small queue every market day. {He} has decided to pass the secret on, and says it is yours, because you were the first to be paid in radishes.

choices.text: Learn the secret recipe

effects.log: Salt, sugar, a little rice wine and a lot of patience. {npc} makes you swear never to write it down. You write it down that night, just in case, and burn it in the morning.

choices.text: Say the secret should stay with the stall

mem.note: left the radish to the stall

effects.log: {npc} thinks about it, and teaches it to the young neighbour who helps at the stall instead. The radish goes on.

events.text: The old well has gone sour, and your father, {npc}, has decided to dig a new one in the yard, by hand, because the well-diggers are thieves. {He} has a spade for you.

choices.text: Dig with {npc}

ok.log: Two weeks of mud. At thirty feet the spade rings on wet gravel and water seeps in, clear and cold. {npc} drinks the first cup and passes you the second.

mem.note: dug the dry well with me

fail.log: Two weeks of mud and a hurt back, and at thirty feet: more mud. {npc} hires the well-diggers after all, and pretends it was your idea.

choices.text: Hire the well-diggers secretly (15 taels)

mem.note: paid for the well behind my back

effects.log: The well-diggers say {npc} sent for them. {npc} glares at you, and is very glad of the water.

events.text: {npc} has found something in the mud from the well: an old bronze coin, worn smooth, centuries old. {He} is sure it means something.

choices.text: Take it to the town's scholar

effects.log: The scholar says it is from a dynasty long gone, and probably fell from a pocket at a market that once stood here. {npc} is delighted to have had a market.

choices.text: Hang it on a cord over the well

mem.note: hung the coin over the well

effects.log: It turns in the wind and catches the light. {npc} says the well will never go sour now. It never does.

events.text: The neighbours have been drawing water from {npc}'s well for years now. {npc} wants to carve a name on the well's stone rim, and asks you what it should be.

choices.text: Name it after {npc}

effects.log: {npc} protests, then carves {his} own name, very small, round the side where nobody looks.

choices.text: Call it the Market Well, for the coin

mem.note: named the well for the coin

effects.log: {npc} carves it in big characters. People who come for water ask why, and {npc} tells them about the lost market for an hour each.

events.text: Your father, {npc}, turns up at your door with two fishing rods and no reason, which has never happened in your whole life. You have not really spoken since an old quarrel. {He} holds out a rod.

choices.text: Take the rod and go

effects.log: You fish all afternoon without a word. On the way back {npc} says, 'Good fish.' It is the most either of you has said in years.

choices.text: Ask what this is about

mem.note: asked what the fishing was about

effects.log: {npc} looks at the river and says, 'Fish.' You go fishing. You still do not know, but you have a carp.

events.text: {npc} comes with the rods again. This time, halfway through the afternoon, without looking up from the water, {he} starts to say something about the old quarrel. It is very slow going.

choices.text: Wait, and let {npc} finish

effects.log: It takes an hour. {npc} says sorry once, very fast, into the river. You say it back, slower. Neither of you catches anything.

choices.text: Say sorry first, to save {npc} the trouble

effects.log: {npc} looks at you, stunned, and then says, 'No, no, I was going to say it.' {He} says it anyway. You both feel lighter.

events.text: The fishing has become a thing you do, you and {npc}, once a season, by the same bend. Today {npc} brings a third rod, a small one.

choices.text: Ask who it is for

effects.log: 'For whoever comes next,' {npc} says. 'Some things should not take forty years.'

choices.text: Leave the third rod by the bend for a stranger

effects.log: You prop it against the willow. Next season it is gone, and a bucket with two fish is in its place.

events.text: Your father, {npc}, is too old to be on a roof, and is on the roof. A tile has slipped and {he} will not wait for the tiler. {He} calls down for you to hold the ladder.

choices.text: Hold the ladder and say nothing

mem.note: held the ladder and trusted me

effects.log: You hold it while {npc} fixes the tile, slowly, perfectly. {He} comes down trembling and triumphant.

choices.text: Go up and fix it with {him}

mem.note: came up on the roof with me

effects.log: {npc} directs, you lift. The tile goes in. {npc} says it was a two-person job all along, which it was not.

events.text: {npc} is on the roof again. Another tile. You are beginning to suspect {he} is loosening them.

choices.text: Climb up and sit with {him}

mem.note: sat on the roof with me

effects.log: You sit on the ridge together. From up here you can see half the county. {npc} admits {he} just likes the view.

choices.text: Build {npc} a bench on the hill instead

mem.note: built me a bench with a view

effects.log: A bench on the hill above the house, with the same view. {npc} complains that it is too comfortable, and is there every evening.

events.text: No tiles have slipped in a long while. {npc} sits on the hill bench most evenings now, and today {he} waves you up and pats the seat.

choices.text: Sit and watch the sun go down

effects.log: {npc} names every roof in the village and who mended it. Most of them, it turns out, {npc} did.

choices.text: Bring a ladder up as a joke

mem.note: brought a ladder up the hill

effects.log: {npc} laughs until {he} wheezes, and then says the joke is on you, because the hen house roof really does need doing.

events.text: Your grandmother, {npc}, is embroidering a tiger on a child's cap, and says you are old enough to learn. {He} gives you a needle, a scrap of red cloth and endless patience.

choices.text: Embroider a tiger

effects.log: Your tiger has the face of a worried cat and one ear. {npc} says it is a very fierce tiger, for a cat.

choices.text: Embroider {npc} instead

effects.log: You stitch a small grey person with a needle. {npc} laughs so much {he} pricks a finger.

events.text: {npc} shows you something: inside the lining of your winter coat, stitched in, is your crooked tiger from last year. 'For protection,' {he} says. 'The ugly ones work best.'

choices.text: Stitch a tiger for {npc}'s coat too

mem.note: stitched me a tiger for my coat

effects.log: It takes you a month. This one has two ears. {npc} sews it into {his} own lining and pats it every morning.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to teach you the proper stitches

effects.log: Satin stitch, knot stitch, the tiger's stripes in split stitch. By winter your tigers look like tigers.

events.text: {npc}'s eyes are too weak for needlework now. {He} hands you the basket of threads and the old pattern for the tiger cap, and asks you to finish the one {he} started for the newest baby in the family.

choices.text: Finish it, stitch by stitch

effects.log: The tiger is half {npc}'s, half yours, and you can see exactly where. The baby wears it all winter.

choices.text: Stitch a crooked one, for luck

mem.note: stitched a crooked tiger for luck

effects.log: The tiger has one ear and a worried face, on purpose. {npc} feels it with {his} fingers and laughs. 'The ugly ones work best.'

events.arc: The Cat Who Was Great-Uncle Bo
events.text: Your grandmother, {npc}, has decided the new stray cat is the reincarnation of great-uncle Bo, who died the winter before last. The cat, like great-uncle Bo, sleeps all day and takes the best seat.

choices.text: Agree that it is great-uncle Bo

effects.log: You bow to the cat. The cat accepts this. {npc} is enormously pleased and feeds it fish. It may in fact be great-uncle Bo.

choices.text: Point out that the cat is a girl

effects.log: {npc} says great-uncle Bo was always full of surprises. The cat keeps the best seat.

events.arc: The Cat Who Was Great-Uncle Bo
events.text: Great-uncle Bo has been caught stealing the festival fish, which, {npc} says, is exactly what great-uncle Bo did in life. {He} wants you to give the cat a stern talking-to, as the eldest grandchild present.

choices.text: Give the cat a stern talking-to

effects.log: You lecture the cat on family honour. It yawns. {npc} says that is exactly how great-uncle Bo took criticism.

choices.text: Buy another fish and say nothing (2 taels)

effects.log: You buy a new fish. {npc} winks at you, and gives the cat the head.

events.arc: The Cat Who Was Great-Uncle Bo
events.text: The cat is old now, as old as cats go, and sleeps in {npc}'s lap all day. {npc} has started telling the cat stories about great-uncle Bo, as if to remind it.

choices.text: Sit and listen to the stories too

mem.note: listened to the stories of Bo

effects.log: You learn more about great-uncle Bo in an afternoon than in your whole life. The cat sleeps through all of it, which is very in character.

choices.text: Bring the cat a fish, for great-uncle Bo

effects.log: The cat eats it, slowly, with great dignity. {npc} says great-uncle Bo never once said thank you either.

events.text: Your grandmother, {npc}, has realised that every recipe in the family is in {his} head and nowhere else, and {his} head, {he} says, is getting full of holes. {He} wants you to write them down.

choices.text: Write every recipe {npc} says

effects.log: {npc} does not measure anything. A handful, a pinch, until it smells right. You write: until it smells right. Forty times.

choices.text: Cook each one beside {npc} and measure

effects.log: You weigh {npc}'s handfuls when {he} is not looking. The recipes come out exact. {npc} says they will taste wrong, written like that.

events.text: {npc} has remembered a recipe from {his} own grandmother's time: a soup nobody has made in sixty years. {He} is not sure of the ingredients. It needs a mountain herb and a river fish.

choices.text: Find the ingredients and cook it

ok.log: The soup smells, says {npc}, exactly right. {He} drinks a bowl with {his} eyes shut and is somewhere else for a while, a long way back.

mem.note: tried to cook the old soup

fail.log: It is not quite right. {npc} says it is close enough, and that the real one was probably not that good either.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to describe the old kitchen instead

effects.log: {npc} talks about a kitchen sixty years gone, down to the cracked bowl. You write that down too, at the front of the book.

events.text: The book of recipes is finished. {npc} holds it in {his} lap and turns the pages without reading them, then hands it to you. 'Make them wrong sometimes,' {he} says. 'That is how they get better.'

choices.text: Cook the first recipe in the book for {npc}

mem.note: cooked from the book for me

effects.log: You make it exactly as written. {npc} tastes it and says it needs more salt, and you add salt to the book.

choices.text: Make copies for every branch of the family (5 taels)

effects.log: Six copies, bound in blue cloth. {npc} writes {his} name inside every one, carefully, in large characters.

events.text: Your grandfather, {npc}, tells you about the great war against the northern raiders, and how {he} held a bridge alone for three days. Last year it was two days, and a river.

choices.text: Ask for every detail

effects.log: {npc} tells you about the bridge, the raiders, the horse {he} rode. The horse's name changes twice. It is the best story you have ever heard.

choices.text: Ask whether it was two days or three

mem.note: counted the days of my war

effects.log: {npc} looks at you sharply, then laughs. 'Three. The second time I tell it, it is three.'

events.text: Clearing out an old chest, you find {npc}'s army papers. {npc} was not a soldier. {npc} was the army's cook, for nine years, and received a commendation for feeding a whole regiment through a winter siege.

choices.text: Tell {npc} you found the papers

effects.log: {npc} is quiet for a while. Then {he} tells you the real story: the siege, the frozen rice, the soldiers {he} kept alive with soup. It is a better story.

choices.text: Put the papers back and say nothing

effects.log: The bridge is three days again at New Year. You let it be three days. There is more than one kind of holding a bridge.

events.text: {npc} wants to cook the siege soup once more, the one that kept a regiment alive, and asks you to be the regiment.

choices.text: Eat it all and ask for more

effects.log: It is terrible: frozen rice, salt and old cabbage. You eat three bowls. {npc} says the soldiers said the same thing, and meant it.

choices.text: Help {npc} make it better

effects.log: You add ginger, and an egg. {npc} says if {he} had had eggs, the war would have been over in a week.

events.text: Your grandfather, {npc}, keeps a singing cricket in a little gourd by the stove, and its singing has gone thin and old. {He} asks if you will catch {him} a new one in the autumn grass.

choices.text: Catch a cricket that really sings

ok.log: You lie in the grass for a whole evening until you find the loudest one. {npc} holds the gourd to {his} ear and smiles like a boy.

fail.log: You catch a beetle. It does not sing. {npc} keeps it anyway, out of politeness, and names it.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to come and catch one with you

mem.note: lay in the grass with me

effects.log: {npc} creaks down into the grass beside you. You catch nothing, and {npc} tells you about every cricket {he} ever owned.

events.text: The cricket in the gourd sings every evening now, and the whole house listens. {npc} wants to carve a new gourd for it, and needs young eyes for the fine work.

choices.text: Carve the lid with {npc}

effects.log: A tiny carved lid with a moon and a reed. Your knife slips once and the moon has a bite out of it. {npc} says that is how you know it is a real moon.

choices.text: Paint the gourd instead

effects.log: You paint the gourd with autumn grass. The cricket sings louder, or {npc} says it does.

events.text: Autumn again, and {npc} cannot get down into the grass any more. {He} holds out the carved gourd with the bitten moon. 'You know how,' {he} says.

choices.text: Catch the loudest one in the field

effects.log: It takes all evening. When you come back, {npc} is asleep by the stove, and you put the gourd by {his} ear. In the morning {he} says {he} dreamed of crickets.

choices.text: Bring a child to learn how

mem.note: taught the next one to catch crickets

effects.log: You teach a small one of the house to lie still in the grass. The child catches a beetle. {npc} keeps it, and names it.

events.text: Your grandfather, {npc}, has bought the wood for {his} own coffin, as the old custom is, while {he} is still well. It is a beautiful slab of cypress, and {he} needs help carrying it home.

choices.text: Carry it home with {npc}

effects.log: It is very heavy. {npc} sits on it twice on the way to rest, and says it is very comfortable, which is a good sign.

choices.text: Hire a cart (3 taels)

effects.log: {npc} rides home sitting on the slab like a lord. Half the lane comes out to wave.

events.text: The cypress slab has been in the yard for two years. {npc} has turned it into a bench, and sits on it every evening, and invites people to sit on it with {him}. The neighbours find this alarming.

choices.text: Sit on the bench with {npc}

effects.log: It is a very good bench. {npc} says {he} intends to get a great deal of use out of it first.

choices.text: Carve a pattern on the bench's edge

effects.log: You carve pine branches along the edge. {npc} says the pine is for long life, and the joke is very good.

events.text: {npc}'s cypress bench has outlasted three other benches in the lane and is still in use. Today {npc} says {he} has decided not to be buried in it after all. 'Too good a bench,' {he} says. 'I will buy pine.'

choices.text: Promise the bench stays in the yard

effects.log: {npc} nods. 'Then people can sit on me after,' {he} says, and laughs so hard {he} has to sit down, on the bench.

choices.text: Put a cushion on it, finally

effects.log: {npc} declares the cushion an insult to the cypress, and uses it every day.

events.text: {npc} drags you up the ladder into the hayloft and shows you a secret: a kingdom made of straw, with a throne of sacks, a treasury of shiny pebbles and laws scratched on a beam. 'You can be the general,' {he} says.

choices.text: Be the general

effects.log: You defend the kingdom against the cat for a whole summer. The laws on the beam grow to forty, mostly about the cat.

choices.text: Demand to be co-ruler

effects.log: {npc} thinks about it and agrees, on the condition that you share the pebbles. The kingdom has two thrones from then on.

events.text: Years later, mending the barn roof, you and {npc} find the beam. The laws are still there. Law nine: No crying in the kingdom unless the cat started it.

choices.text: Read all forty laws out loud

mem.note: read the old laws with me

effects.log: You read every one. By law thirty {npc} is laughing so hard {he} has to sit in the hay. The pebbles are still in the treasury.

choices.text: Scratch a forty-first law

mem.note: added a law to the kingdom

effects.log: Law forty-one: The kingdom stands. {npc} adds {his} mark under it, like a seal.

events.text: {npc} brings the children of the house to the barn and points up at the hayloft. 'There is a kingdom up there,' {he} says. 'And this one was its general.' The children look at you with new respect.

choices.text: Show them the kingdom

mem.note: gave the kingdom to the children

effects.log: You climb up with them. The children declare new laws within the hour, mostly about you. {npc} sits at the bottom of the ladder, very pleased.

choices.text: Hand them the pebbles of the treasury

effects.log: The children divide the pebbles with great seriousness and some fighting. The kingdom has new rulers.

events.text: {npc} needs to borrow your best coat. {He} has a meeting with a matchmaker's candidate tomorrow and owns nothing that is not patched. {He} swears on everything that it will come back spotless.

choices.text: Lend the coat

effects.log: The coat comes back two days later, spotless except for one small tear and a smell of plum sauce. {npc} is glowing. The meeting went well.

choices.text: Take {npc} to buy a coat of {his} own (8 taels)

effects.log: You haggle for a decent coat in a good blue. {npc} stares at the stranger in the tailor's mirror for a long time.

events.text: {npc} is getting married, to the matchmaker's candidate from the plum sauce meeting. {He} wants you to stand beside {him} at the wedding, and has a coat for you to wear, borrowed.

choices.text: Wear the borrowed coat proudly

mem.note: stood beside me at the wedding

effects.log: It is too big and smells of camphor. You stand beside {npc} through the whole wedding and do not tear it once.

choices.text: Wear your own old coat, the one with the tear

mem.note: wore the torn coat to my wedding

effects.log: {npc} sees the mended tear and laughs out loud in the middle of the ceremony. The in-laws are puzzled. It is the right coat.

events.text: {npc}'s own child is old enough for a matchmaker now, and has nothing to wear. {npc} arrives at your door, not quite able to ask.

choices.text: Get out the old good coat

mem.note: lent the coat a second time

effects.log: It still fits, mostly. The child goes off in it, and comes back with a small tear and a smell of plum sauce, and glowing.

choices.text: Take them both to the tailor (8 taels)

effects.log: A new coat in a good blue. {npc} stands in the tailor's mirror behind the child and says nothing, because there is nothing to say.

events.text: {npc} has a plan: a noodle stall by the river gate, where the porters eat. {He} has worked out everything except the money for a cart and a pot, and is looking at you very hard.

choices.text: Put up the money (20 taels)

effects.log: You buy a cart, a pot and a sign. {npc} cooks a test bowl for you, so hot your eyes water. 'Good?' 'Good.'

choices.text: Help build the cart yourself

effects.log: You build it from an old door and two wheels. It leans. {npc} paints it red and says the lean is part of the charm.

events.text: The noodle stall by the river gate has a queue of porters at dawn. {npc} wants you to taste a new broth {he} is working on, and to tell the truth this time.

choices.text: Tell the truth: too much ginger

mem.note: told me the truth about the broth

effects.log: {npc} glares, tries again, and the next broth is the best thing you have ever eaten. The porters agree.

choices.text: Say it is perfect

effects.log: It is not perfect. The porters tell {npc} so the next morning, at length. {npc} comes back to you, furious, and you both laugh.

events.text: {npc}'s noodle stall has become a small shop with a roof and four tables. Over the door, carved in wood, is the stall's name, and it is your name.

choices.text: Eat a bowl at every table, one each year

effects.log: {npc} says that is a contract. Every year you eat at the next table. It is an excellent contract.

choices.text: Ask {npc} why

mem.note: asked why the shop has their name

effects.log: 'Because you looked at me hard, once, and said yes,' {npc} says, and puts a second egg in your bowl.

events.text: {npc} marks heights on the kitchen doorframe with a knife, and has caught up with you. {He} is standing on tiptoe and swearing {he} is not.

choices.text: Insist on a fair measure

effects.log: Heels down. You are still taller, by a fingernail. {npc} declares it a draw and stomps off.

choices.text: Let the tiptoe stand

effects.log: {npc}'s mark goes above yours. {npc} looks at it, and at you, and says, 'Next year it will be real.'

events.text: The doorframe again. This year {npc} is truly taller, by a hand, and is being unbearable about it.

choices.text: Grow a beard of soot and claim wisdom instead

effects.log: You draw a beard with soot and claim that the old outrank the tall. The kitchen laughs. {npc} draws one too.

choices.text: Congratulate {npc}, sincerely

effects.log: {npc} is so surprised by sincerity that {he} stops being unbearable for nearly a week.

events.text: You and {npc} are back in the old kitchen, grown, and the doorframe is still there, covered with knife marks: yours, {npc}'s, and a new row, much lower, for the next ones.

choices.text: Measure each other one last time

mem.note: measured me at the doorframe again

effects.log: Heels down. Exactly where you were at eighteen, both of you, maybe a little lower. You add the marks anyway.

choices.text: Carve both names beside the old marks

mem.note: carved our names at the doorframe

effects.log: You carve the names so the new ones will know whose marks are whose. {npc} insists on carving the word tiptoe beside one of {his} own.

events.arc: A Sibling at the Edge of the Empire
events.text: {npc} is leaving to work for a salt merchant at the far edge of the empire, a month's road away. On the last evening {he} sits with you on the step and does not say goodbye.

choices.text: Promise to write every season

effects.log: {npc} nods. 'Every season,' {he} repeats, so you both remember. In the morning there is just a gap on the step.

choices.text: Give {npc} something from home

effects.log: You give {npc} a handful of earth from the yard in a twist of paper. {He} pretends it is silly and puts it next to {his} heart.

events.arc: A Sibling at the Edge of the Empire
events.text: A letter from {npc}, in a hand that has got more grown-up. The salt flats, the camels, a friend who is half bandit. At the end: I still have the paper of earth. Is the plum tree still there?

choices.text: Send back a plum from the tree, dried

mem.note: sent me a plum from home

effects.log: It travels a month and arrives as something like a stone. {npc} writes that it tasted exactly like home and also like a stone.

choices.text: Write back with every bit of home news

effects.log: You write ten pages: who married, whose goat escaped. {npc} reads it, {he} writes, on a camel, out loud, to the half-bandit.

events.arc: A Sibling at the Edge of the Empire
events.text: {npc} comes home, years later, brown as a nut, with a salt-crusted bag and stories for a lifetime. {He} goes straight to the plum tree before anything else.

choices.text: Sit under the plum tree and hear all of it

effects.log: Camels, salt, the half-bandit, who turns out to have been fully a bandit and very kind. You hear it all until the stars come out.

choices.text: Show {npc} the empty spot on the step

mem.note: kept my place on the step

effects.log: The step has never been the same with a gap in it. {npc} sits in the gap. It fits, still.

events.text: The good blue vase is in pieces on the floor and {npc} is standing over it, white as rice. The grown-ups are coming up the path.

choices.text: Say you did it

mem.note: took the blame for the vase

effects.log: You take the scolding and the extra chores. {npc} gives you {his} dessert for a month without a word.

choices.text: Hide the pieces with {npc}

effects.log: You bury the vase under the pear tree. The grown-ups search for weeks. You and {npc} are bound for life by a terrible secret.

events.text: {npc} wants to confess about the vase, after all this time. {He} is nervous, and wants you there.

choices.text: Go with {npc}

effects.log: The grown-ups listen to the whole confession and then admit they always knew, and that the vase was ugly. {npc} is outraged at the wasted years.

choices.text: Talk {npc} out of it

effects.log: Some secrets are better kept, you say. {npc} agrees, relieved. The vase stays a secret, and gets bigger every year in the telling.

events.text: At a family gathering, the old ones are telling stories, and somebody mentions the good blue vase that vanished. {npc} looks at you across the table.

choices.text: Tell the whole story

effects.log: You tell it: the vase, the pear tree, the confession. The whole table howls. The old ones say it really was very ugly.

choices.text: Dig up the pieces with {npc} that night

mem.note: dug up the vase with me

effects.log: You find three blue shards under the pear tree in the moonlight. {npc} keeps one, you keep one, and you put one back.

events.text: Years ago you lent {npc} ten taels. Today {npc} stands at your gate, very formal, with a goat on a rope. 'The debt,' {he} says. 'This is Plum. Plum is worth at least eleven.'

choices.text: Accept Plum gravely

effects.log: Plum moves in, eats your sandals, and turns out to give very good milk. You admit Plum is worth at least eleven.

choices.text: Say the debt was forgiven long ago

effects.log: {npc} says {he} knows, and that is why it is a goat and not silver. Plum moves in anyway.

events.text: Plum the goat has opinions about the household and expresses them by headbutting. {npc} visits to see how {his} payment is getting on, and Plum headbutts {him} into the water trough.

choices.text: Pull {npc} out, laughing

mem.note: pulled me out of the trough

effects.log: {npc} sits dripping in the yard and says Plum is clearly worth twelve now. Plum agrees.

choices.text: Offer to give Plum back

effects.log: {npc} looks at Plum. Plum looks at {npc}. 'No,' {npc} says. 'A debt is a debt.'

events.text: Plum has had kids, three of them. {npc} comes over, very formal, to say {he} would like to borrow ten taels.

choices.text: Lend {npc} the money, and send a kid along (10 taels)

mem.note: lent me silver and a goat

effects.log: {npc} goes home with silver and a small goat. 'Interest,' you say. {npc} says that is not how interest works, and keeps the goat.

choices.text: Pay {npc} in goat

effects.log: You hand over a kid on a rope. 'This is Pear,' you say. {npc} laughs until {he} has to lean on the gate.

events.text: {npc} has come to talk about your parents. They are getting old, and {npc} has been doing most of the caring, and is tired, and did not want to say so.

choices.text: Take every other month

mem.note: took turns caring for our parents

effects.log: You work it out at the kitchen table: you take every other month. {npc} sleeps for the first time in a season.

choices.text: Send silver for a hired helper (15 taels)

effects.log: A good-natured widow comes in every day to help. {npc} is grateful, and a little sad it is not you.

events.text: Your month with the old ones again. {npc} drops by with soup and stays to argue, the way you both did as children, while the old ones listen from their chairs and enjoy it enormously.

choices.text: Argue properly, for the old ones

effects.log: You argue about whose turn it was to feed the hens in a year long ago. The old ones take sides. It is the liveliest the house has been in years.

choices.text: Thank {npc} for the years alone

mem.note: thanked me for the years alone

effects.log: {npc} goes red and says it was nothing, and then says it was not nothing, and then you both drink the soup.

events.text: The house is quiet now; the old ones are gone. You and {npc} sit at their table, which neither of you can bear to sell.

choices.text: Keep the house for both families

mem.note: kept the old house with me

effects.log: You agree to keep it, and meet there every New Year. The table stays where it was.

choices.text: Take one chair each, and let the rest go

mem.note: shared the old chairs with me

effects.log: You take one old chair, {npc} the other. Somehow that is enough.

events.text: Your uncle, {npc}, has invented a machine that cooks rice by itself. It has a water wheel, a bellows and a great many strings. {He} wants a witness for the first test.

choices.text: Witness it

effects.log: The machine cooks the rice, then throws it onto the ceiling. {npc} looks up at the ceiling with deep satisfaction. 'Step one,' {he} says.

choices.text: Suggest fewer strings

effects.log: {npc} removes half the strings. The machine cooks the rice and only throws a little of it. {He} names you assistant inventor.

events.text: {npc}'s latest invention: shoes with springs, for jumping over puddles. {He} cannot try them today, {he} says, because of {his} back. {He} looks at you.

choices.text: Try the spring shoes

ok.log: You clear the puddle by a whole stride and land like a cat. {npc} weeps with joy and makes six more pairs, which all fail.

mem.note: bounced through the puddles for science

fail.log: You land in the puddle, then bounce out of it, then into the next one. The whole lane comes to watch. {npc} takes notes.

choices.text: Suggest springs for the well bucket instead

mem.note: gave me the idea for the bucket

effects.log: {npc} stares at you. Within the week the well bucket comes up by itself, mostly. The lane is astonished.

events.text: {npc} is old now, and has finally invented something that works perfectly: a door that closes by itself on a weight and a pulley. The whole lane has ordered one. {He} wants you to take a share in the business.

choices.text: Take a share and help build them

effects.log: You build forty doors with {npc}. Every one closes softly. {npc} cannot stop opening them.

choices.text: Tell {npc} to keep it all and enjoy it

effects.log: {npc} does, loudly. On your own door {he} installs one for free, with a small bell, and a string that leads nowhere, just for old times.

events.text: Your uncle, {npc}, must give the speech at a cousin's wedding, and has written one. It is forty minutes long and mostly about a pig {he} owned in {his} youth. {He} asks your honest opinion.

choices.text: Cut it down to the pig

effects.log: You cut it to five minutes, all pig. At the wedding the guests laugh until they cry. The cousin says it was the best speech in family history.

choices.text: Help {npc} write about the cousin instead

mem.note: wrote my wedding speech with me

effects.log: You find stories about the cousin as a child, falling in ponds. {npc} reads it with feeling, and also mentions the pig.

events.text: Word has got round. {npc} is now in demand for wedding speeches across three villages, and wants you as {his} writer.

choices.text: Write the speeches, for a share of the gifts

effects.log: You write nine wedding speeches that year. Every one has a pig in it somewhere. {npc} is famous.

choices.text: Teach {npc} to write them alone

mem.note: taught me to write my own

effects.log: It takes a season. {npc}'s own speeches are wilder and better than yours. You go to every wedding to hear them.

events.text: {npc} is to give a speech at your own celebration, and has refused to show you a word of it.

choices.text: Let {npc} speak, and brace yourself

mem.note: listened to my speech for them

effects.log: It is about you as a child, falling in ponds, and then about a pig, and then, at the very end, it is about you as you are, and the room goes quiet.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to leave out the ponds

effects.log: {npc} agrees, and talks about the ponds anyway, for twelve minutes. It is the best speech you have ever heard.

events.text: Your aunt, {npc}, runs a small teahouse by the market, and the festival rush has come and both helpers are sick. {He} ties an apron on you before you can say anything.

choices.text: Pour tea all day

mem.note: poured tea all day for me

effects.log: You pour four hundred cups and remember most orders. By evening {npc} gives you a whole dish of almond cakes and a look of respect.

choices.text: Take the money and keep the accounts

effects.log: You keep the accounts all day without a single mistake. {npc} checks them twice and then hugs you.

events.text: {npc} has a secret: the almond cakes, which made the teahouse famous, come from a recipe that is fading. The old baker who made them has gone, and {npc}'s copies taste wrong.

choices.text: Work out the recipe by taste

ok.log: After a week of almond flour on every surface, you have it: a pinch of salt, and the almonds roasted twice. {npc} tastes one and closes {his} eyes.

mem.note: tried to find the almond cakes

fail.log: You get close. {npc} says close is better than gone, and sells them as the new almond cakes. People like them.

choices.text: Find the old baker and ask

effects.log: The old baker lives with a grandson by the river and is delighted to be asked. The secret is salt and twice-roasted almonds, and a story about a lost love.

events.text: {npc} is giving up the teahouse; the stairs have got too much. {He} hands you the almond cake recipe, written on a scrap of paper, and the old teapot, cracked and mended with silver.

choices.text: Keep the teapot and use it every day

effects.log: Every morning you make tea in {npc}'s teapot. It pours a little crooked. You would not change it.

choices.text: Take the teapot and the recipe to the next owner

effects.log: The new owner is a young couple, nervous. You give them the recipe and the teapot and {npc}'s blessing. The almond cakes go on.

events.text: Your aunt, {npc}, reads fortunes in tea leaves and has never once predicted anything good. Today, peering into your cup, {he} gasps. 'A great disaster is coming. Something will fall.'

choices.text: Thank {npc} and be careful all week

effects.log: On the sixth day a pear falls on your head. {npc} is vindicated and tells everyone.

choices.text: Ask for a second reading

effects.log: {npc} reads the second cup: worse. Something will fall, and it will be wet. A week later you drop a bucket in the well.

events.text: {npc}'s tea-leaf disasters have become the most reliable fortunes in the district, because they are so small. People come from three streets away to hear that they will stub a toe.

choices.text: Become {npc}'s assistant

effects.log: You hand out the cups and look grave. Business doubles. You predict a lost button for a magistrate's clerk and it happens.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to read a good fortune, just once

mem.note: got a good fortune from me at last

effects.log: {npc} peers into the cup for a long time. 'Something good,' {he} says, shocked. That afternoon you find a coin in the road.

events.text: {npc} reads your cup one more time, very slowly, and does not gasp. 'Nothing will fall,' {he} says. 'Everything will hold.'

choices.text: Believe it

effects.log: Everything holds that year: the roof, the well rope, the bridge in the flood. You are almost disappointed.

choices.text: Read {npc}'s cup in return

effects.log: You squint into the leaves. 'Something will fall,' you say. {npc} laughs so hard {he} knocks over the teapot, which falls.

events.text: {npc} is very old now, and today calls you by somebody else's name, a name from long ago, and asks if you have fed the ox. There has been no ox for forty years.

choices.text: Say yes, the ox is fed

effects.log: {npc} relaxes at once and tells you a long story about the ox, who was called Iron and liked turnips. You learn a great deal about Iron.

choices.text: Gently say your own name

effects.log: {npc} looks at you for a long moment, and then laughs. 'Of course. You have the same chin.' {He} tells you whose chin it was.

events.text: {npc} remembers the ox more than the year now. The household has learned to feed Iron every morning, by agreement. {npc} asks you to take the ox to the river.

choices.text: Walk to the river and back with an empty rope

effects.log: You walk the rope to the river and let the ox drink. When you come back {npc} asks how Iron was. Thirsty, you say.

choices.text: Bring {npc} to the river to see

effects.log: You walk {npc} slowly to the river. {He} looks at the water a long time and says, 'Iron liked it here.' Then {he} knows you, clearly, and holds your hand.

events.text: On a clear morning {npc} knows everyone, and the year, and says that {he} has a story for you that is not about the ox.

choices.text: Listen to every word

mem.note: heard my story on a clear day

effects.log: It is about your own childhood, something you never knew: a night {npc} sat up with you in a fever until dawn. {He} remembers it exactly.

choices.text: Write it down as {npc} speaks

effects.log: You write it all down. That night {npc} forgets again, and asks about the ox, and you have the story in your sleeve.

events.text: {npc} has decided to have a portrait painted, for the hall, before it is too late, and has saved for it for years. {He} wants you to choose the painter.

choices.text: Choose the famous painter (15 taels)

effects.log: You add silver to {npc}'s savings for the best painter in town. The portrait is very grand, and looks like a minister. {npc} is thrilled.

choices.text: Choose the honest young painter

effects.log: The young painter paints {npc} exactly: the warts, the squint, the smile. The household is horrified. {npc} loves it.

events.text: Visitors to the hall stop at {npc}'s portrait and say things. {npc} sits nearby on purpose to hear them, and asks you to sit too.

choices.text: Sit and listen together

mem.note: listened to the visitors with me

effects.log: A child says the portrait looks kind. A merchant says it looks like it knows about debts. {npc} is delighted with both.

choices.text: Tell the visitors stories about {npc}

effects.log: You turn every visit into a story about {npc}. By the end of the year the portrait is the most famous thing in the house.

events.text: {npc} has looked at the portrait every day for years, and now says {he} would like one more thing on it: you, standing behind, painted small.

choices.text: Have the painter add you

mem.note: stood behind me in the portrait

effects.log: The painter adds you, small, behind {npc}'s shoulder, very much yourself. {npc} looks at the two of you for a long time.

choices.text: Say the portrait should stay {npc}'s alone

effects.log: {npc} thinks, and agrees, and then makes you stand behind the portrait for an hour while {he} looks at it, just to see.

events.text: {npc} has dropped the family's oldest heirloom, a silver hairpin from four generations back, down the well. {He} is frantic. The well is deep and cold.

choices.text: Go down on the rope

mem.note: went down the well for the hairpin

ok.log: You go down into the cold, feel about in the mud with your toes, and come up with the hairpin and a very old copper coin. {npc} cries over both.

mem.note: went down the well for me

fail.log: You go down, freeze, and come up empty-handed and blue. {npc} wraps you in every blanket in the house.

choices.text: Fish for it with a magnet stone and a string

effects.log: It takes all day. On the hundredth try the hairpin comes up on the string. {npc} cannot believe a stone did it.

events.text: {npc} wants the hairpin mended and polished, and asks you to take it to a silversmith in the town, because {he} does not trust {his} own hands with it any more.

choices.text: Take it and watch the work

mem.note: found the old name in the hairpin

effects.log: The silversmith polishes it, and finds a tiny name engraved inside the curve: the great-great-grandmother's. Nobody living knew it was there.

choices.text: Have a copy made too (6 taels)

effects.log: Now there are two hairpins. {npc} keeps the old one and gives the copy to the youngest of the house, which starts a small war.

events.text: {npc} gives you the silver hairpin, wrapped in red cloth. 'You went into the well for it,' {he} says. 'It is yours to hand on.'

choices.text: Keep it safe for the next one

effects.log: You put it in your box of best things. On cold days you hold it, and think of the well.

choices.text: Have the old name re-cut, and add {npc}'s

mem.note: had my name cut in the hairpin

effects.log: Two names inside the curve now. {npc} holds it to the light and reads them both, very slowly.

events.text: {npc} has decided the whole house must be cleaned before the year turns, every corner, and you are the army. Under the oldest cupboard you find a box nobody remembers.

choices.text: Open the box

effects.log: Inside: a wooden sword, a letter never sent, and a dried flower. {npc} goes very quiet, and then says the cleaning can wait an hour.

choices.text: Give the box to {npc} unopened

effects.log: {npc} takes it into the next room. You hear {him} laughing, then nothing, then laughing again.

events.text: Spring cleaning again. {npc} has decided that this year you will finally clear the attic, where the house keeps everything it cannot throw away.

choices.text: Clear the attic, and keep only what is loved

effects.log: A cradle, a kite, twenty broken chairs. You keep the cradle and the kite and burn the chairs, and {npc} cries over one of them.

choices.text: Turn the attic into a reading room

effects.log: You clear it, sweep it and put in a mat and a lamp. {npc} says it is a waste, and is found up there every afternoon.

events.text: The spring cleaning has become a tradition with its own rules: {npc} gives orders, everyone obeys, and at the end the forgotten box is opened, and something is put in.

choices.text: Put in something of your own

effects.log: You put in a letter to whoever opens it next. {npc} wants to read it. You say no. {npc} is very pleased about that.

choices.text: Let the youngest choose what goes in

effects.log: The youngest puts in a beetle in a jar, with great ceremony. {npc} says that is perfect, and makes sure the jar has air holes.

events.text: {npc} wants the sunny bed by the wall for peonies. You want it for cabbages. Neither of you will give way, and the bed has stood empty for a month while you both argue about it.

choices.text: Plant half and half

effects.log: Peonies on the left, cabbages on the right, a line of stones between like a border. You both watch the line suspiciously all spring.

choices.text: Give {npc} the bed

effects.log: Peonies, enormous and red. {npc} picks the first one and puts it in a cabbage pot on your table, which is either a peace offering or a joke.

events.text: The garden border war has gone on for years. This spring, a cabbage has appeared on {npc}'s side, and a peony on yours, and neither of you admits to planting them.

choices.text: Plant another cabbage among the peonies

effects.log: The next morning there are two peonies on your side. By midsummer the bed is hopelessly mixed and very beautiful.

choices.text: Confess to the peony

effects.log: {npc} confesses to the cabbage at once. You both laugh in the garden until the neighbour looks over the wall.

events.text: The old bed by the wall is a jumble of peonies and cabbages, as it has been for years. {npc} has put a bench in the middle of it, facing nowhere in particular.

choices.text: Sit on the bench with {npc}

mem.note: sat in our garden with me

effects.log: From the bench you can see both the flowers and the dinner. {npc} says that was always the point.

choices.text: Cook a cabbage soup with a peony in the bowl

effects.log: {npc} eats it to the last leaf and says it is the best soup {he} has ever been insulted with.

events.text: {npc} snores. Not a little: like a carpenter sawing through a door. {npc} denies it absolutely.

choices.text: Prove it, with witnesses

effects.log: You bring the neighbour's child to listen at the window. The child runs home and tells the whole lane. {npc} is furious for a day and then laughs.

choices.text: Buy a herbal pillow (3 taels)

effects.log: The pillow is filled with dried chrysanthemum. The snoring changes key, but does not stop. The bedroom smells lovely.

choices.text: Learn to sleep through it

mem.note: learned to sleep through my snoring

effects.log: It takes a season. Then, one night, {npc} is away, and you cannot sleep at all for the silence.

events.text: {npc} has turned the tables: you snore too, apparently, and {npc} has kept a record, in a little book, with comments.

choices.text: Read the book

effects.log: Night of the third: like a goose in a well. Night of the ninth: a whole orchestra. You laugh so hard {npc} has to slap your back.

choices.text: Start your own book

effects.log: Two books now, one each side of the bed. The comments get more poetic every month. Some are rather good.

events.text: The snoring books fill a whole shelf now. On a winter night {npc} reads one of the old ones aloud by the lamp, the voice going soft at the funny bits.

choices.text: Listen until you fall asleep

mem.note: fell asleep to the old book

effects.log: You fall asleep to your own snoring being read aloud. {npc} writes a new entry: fell asleep during the reading. A good night.

choices.text: Read one of yours back

mem.note: read the old book back to me

effects.log: You read the night of the goose in the well. {npc} laughs until {he} snorts, which you note down at once.

events.text: {npc} has been disappearing every afternoon and coming home smelling of garlic, and will not say where. The neighbours are beginning to look at you with pity.

choices.text: Follow {npc} one afternoon

effects.log: {npc} goes to the old cook behind the temple and takes a lesson in noodles. You creep home before you are seen, very ashamed and very pleased.

choices.text: Trust {npc} and say nothing

effects.log: You say nothing for a month. The neighbours stop looking at you. You do not ask, which is harder than it sounds.

events.text: The secret is out: {npc} cooks you a dinner of hand-pulled noodles, wobbly and uneven and made with enormous care. {npc} watches you take the first bite.

choices.text: Eat every noodle and ask for more

mem.note: asked for more of my noodles

effects.log: There is no more. {npc} made only the one bowl, it took four hours, and {he} is delighted you want more.

choices.text: Ask to learn too

effects.log: {npc} teaches you what the old cook taught. Your noodles are worse. You both eat them anyway, laughing, flour everywhere.

events.text: Noodles have become what your house is known for. On festival days the neighbours bring bowls, and {npc} pulls noodles in the yard with the old cook's own movements, and you serve.

choices.text: Take over the pulling this year

effects.log: {npc} supervises, very critical. Your noodles have come a long way. {npc} admits it in front of the whole lane.

choices.text: Carry a bowl to the old cook behind the temple

effects.log: The old cook is very old now. The cook eats every noodle and says {npc} was the best pupil in forty years, and the second best is you.

events.text: {npc} comes home from the market with a goose under one arm. It was meant to be dinner. It is now called General Wen and is sitting in the best chair.

choices.text: Accept General Wen into the household

effects.log: General Wen guards the gate better than any dog, bites the tax clerk and lays one egg a week, which {npc} cooks for you with great ceremony.

choices.text: Insist General Wen goes in the yard

mem.note: tried to keep the goose out

effects.log: General Wen goes in the yard. General Wen stands at the door every evening and honks until {npc} lets the goose in.

events.text: General Wen has chased off a thief. The whole lane is talking. {npc} is insufferably proud of the goose.

choices.text: Have a little collar made for the goose (2 taels)

effects.log: General Wen wears a red collar with a brass bell. {npc} weeps slightly. The goose bites the tailor.

choices.text: Admit General Wen is a hero

mem.note: admitted the goose is a hero

effects.log: {npc} makes you say it in front of the goose. You say it. General Wen accepts.

events.text: General Wen is very old for a goose, and walks slowly now, and sleeps by the stove. {npc} sits up with the old bird some nights.

choices.text: Sit up with them both

mem.note: sat up with the old goose

effects.log: General Wen puts that long neck across your knee and sleeps. {npc} says the goose has never done that for anyone else.

choices.text: Make the old goose a bed of rice straw

effects.log: General Wen sleeps in the straw bed by the stove all winter, warm and honking quietly in dreams. {npc} watches you build it and says nothing, which says everything.

events.text: {npc} has a fever, a bad one, and lies in the dark muttering about hens. The physician says three nights will decide it, and it will be decided at home.

choices.text: Sit up three nights

mem.note: sat up three nights with me

effects.log: You change the cloths and spoon the broth and listen to a great deal about hens. On the third dawn the fever breaks, and {npc} asks why you look so terrible.

choices.text: Bring the best physician in town (10 taels)

effects.log: The physician comes twice a day with bitter tea. {npc} complains about the tea, which the physician says is an excellent sign.

events.text: Now it is you with the fever, and {npc} in the chair by the bed, and it is your turn to mutter about hens.

choices.text: Let {npc} nurse you

effects.log: You remember very little, only a voice telling you, over and over, that the hens are fine. When you wake, {npc} is asleep in the chair holding your hand.

choices.text: Insist you are fine and get up

mem.note: tried to get up too soon

effects.log: You get up and fall down. {npc} puts you back to bed with great force and does not leave the chair again for three days.

events.text: A winter cough has both of you this year, and you lie in the same bed coughing at each other like two old crows, each telling the other to drink the tea.

choices.text: Drink the tea first, to set an example

effects.log: It is terrible. {npc} drinks it too, to show you {he} is braver. You both get better in a week, competing.

choices.text: Hire the neighbour's child to bring broth (2 taels)

effects.log: The child brings broth twice a day and stays to tell you about the hens. Everyone is very well informed.

choices.text: Tell old stories until you both fall asleep

effects.log: You get halfway through the story of how you met and argue about every detail. You fall asleep still arguing.

events.text: {npc} admits, over supper, that {he} has never seen the sea. {He} says it lightly, like a joke, but {he} says it twice.

choices.text: Promise to go one day

effects.log: {npc} smiles and says one day, and you both know how one days go. But you put a copper in a jar on the shelf that night, and the next.

choices.text: Go now, while you can (20 taels)

effects.log: Ten days by cart. On the eleventh {npc} stands on the sand in the wind and does not say anything at all. You stay until the tide comes in over your feet.

events.text: The jar on the shelf is full of coppers, or the memory of the sea is still in the house, and {npc} has started collecting shells from pedlars, which is a sign.

choices.text: Go to the sea again, further south (20 taels)

mem.note: took me to the warm sea

effects.log: Warm sea this time, and blue, and full of small fish. {npc} wades in up to the knees and shrieks at the fish.

choices.text: Buy {npc} the biggest shell in the market (4 taels)

mem.note: gave me the sea in a shell

effects.log: {npc} holds it to an ear and listens to the sea in it every evening. Which is nearly the same, {he} says, which is not true, and kind.

choices.text: Draw the sea for {npc} on the wall

effects.log: You paint a terrible sea on the kitchen wall. {npc} adds a boat, then a fish, then a whale. The whole wall is sea by spring.

events.text: {npc} is too old for ten days in a cart now. But {he} has the shells, and the painted wall, and tonight {he} asks you to tell {him} the sea again.

choices.text: Tell it, wave by wave

effects.log: The wind, the sand, the tide over your feet. {npc} listens with eyes shut and says, at the end, that it is just how {he} remembers it.

choices.text: Pour a bowl of salt water and sit with your feet in it

mem.note: made a sea in a bowl

effects.log: Two old people with their feet in a bowl of salt water, laughing. It is very nearly the sea.

events.text: The roof leaks over the bed, and you and {npc} have a serious quarrel about money: you want to mend it properly, {npc} wants to patch it and buy a cow.

choices.text: Patch it and buy the cow

effects.log: The cow is excellent. The patch lasts until the first big storm, when you both sleep under the table.

choices.text: Mend it properly

effects.log: The roof is perfect. {npc} sulks about the cow for a month, then admits it is nice to sleep in a dry bed.

choices.text: Do both, and work extra this year

mem.note: worked double for the roof and the cow

effects.log: You take on extra work all summer, and so does {npc}. A dry roof and a cow by autumn. You are both exhausted and smug.

events.text: The roof quarrel has become a joke between you. Every spending decision is now settled by the question: is it a roof or a cow?

choices.text: Decide the next one is a cow

mem.note: agreed the pot was a cow

effects.log: A good iron pot: definitely a cow. {npc} agrees at once. The pot makes excellent soup for twenty years.

choices.text: Decide the next one is a roof

mem.note: agreed the door was a roof

effects.log: A new door: roof. {npc} agrees, then hangs a little carved cow on it.

events.text: A young couple in the lane are quarrelling about money, loudly, through the wall. {npc} catches your eye across the table.

choices.text: Go round and explain about roofs and cows

effects.log: The young couple listen, baffled, then laugh, then stop shouting. A month later they buy a cow.

choices.text: Leave them to it, and laugh quietly

mem.note: laughed at the young ones with me

effects.log: You and {npc} sit in the dark listening and laughing into your sleeves. Some things everyone has to find out alone.

events.text: {npc} has bought a novel from a pedlar, a fat one with a broken spine, about an outlaw band in the marshes, and wants you to read it aloud, a chapter a night.

choices.text: Read with all the voices

mem.note: read to me with the voices

effects.log: You give the outlaws terrible accents. {npc} laughs so much that the first chapter takes three nights.

choices.text: Take turns, one chapter each

effects.log: {npc} reads in a whisper and you in a bellow. The outlaws sound very different night to night. Neither of you minds.

events.text: Chapter sixty of the novel. A favourite outlaw dies. {npc} closes the book and will not open it again for a week.

choices.text: Read ahead and promise it gets better

effects.log: You read ahead in secret and come back and promise. {npc} does not believe you, then does. You go on.

choices.text: Hold a small funeral for the outlaw

mem.note: held a funeral for the outlaw

effects.log: You burn a twist of paper for the outlaw in the yard. {npc} gives a speech. The neighbours think somebody has died.

events.text: The novel is finished, after years of chapters. {npc} holds the last page and looks at you. 'Again?' {he} says. 'From the start?'

choices.text: Start again from chapter one

mem.note: started the novel again with me

effects.log: The outlaws sound older this time, and so do you. The first chapter still takes three nights.

choices.text: Buy a new novel (3 taels)

mem.note: bought a new novel to read

effects.log: A novel about a monkey who goes to the west. {npc} reads the first chapter in a monkey voice nobody could have expected.

events.text: You are going to {npc}'s home village for the first time as family. {npc}'s relatives, {he} warns, will test you. There is a great-aunt in particular.

choices.text: Pass the great-aunt's tests

ok.log: The great-aunt makes you carry water, eat a pepper whole and recite your ancestors. You do all three. The great-aunt says, to {npc}, 'Acceptable.' {npc} says that is the highest praise in the village.

fail.log: You fail the pepper. You cry for an hour. The great-aunt, to everyone's astonishment, laughs and gives you honey, and says you are honest at least.

choices.text: Bring the great-aunt a gift from home (5 taels)

effects.log: A good cloth from your own market. The great-aunt inspects it for flaws for an hour, finds none, and is silent, which {npc} says is a triumph.

events.text: The village again, for a festival. The great-aunt sits you close by at the feast, which is either an honour or a trap.

choices.text: Talk to the great-aunt all evening

effects.log: It turns out the great-aunt loves rude jokes. You have three. By the end of the evening you are the great-aunt's favourite and {npc} is jealous.

choices.text: Help in the kitchen with the village

effects.log: You peel and wash and carry with all the cousins. Nobody tests you any more. {npc} watches from the door, smiling.

events.text: A letter from {npc}'s village: the great-aunt is very old, and has asked that you come, specifically you, to hear something.

choices.text: Go at once

effects.log: The great-aunt tells you the village's oldest rude joke, which has been passed down for two hundred years. You are now its keeper. {npc} is speechless.

choices.text: Send {npc} with a gift and a letter

effects.log: {npc} comes back and says the great-aunt read your letter twice and said, 'Acceptable.' {npc} cried.

events.text: Mending a coat of {npc}'s, you find a letter sewn into the lining, yellowed, addressed to you, from before you were married. It was never sent.

choices.text: Read it

mem.note: found the letter and sewed it back

effects.log: It is shy, clumsy and very sincere, and it says everything {npc} has never managed to say aloud. You read it twice and sew it back exactly where it was.

choices.text: Give it to {npc} unopened

mem.note: gave me back my letter unread

effects.log: {npc} goes bright red, takes it and hides it, and is very kind to you all week, suspiciously.

events.text: On your anniversary there is an envelope under your bowl: the old letter, at last, sent. On the back {npc} has written: Late. Sorry.

choices.text: Write an answer to the old letter

effects.log: You answer it as if you were twenty again. {npc} reads your answer in the yard and has to sit down on the well.

choices.text: Read it aloud to {npc}

effects.log: {npc} hides behind a sleeve for the whole letter. At the end, from behind the sleeve: 'It is still true.'

events.text: Both letters, the old one and your answer, are in a box now, with others. Tonight {npc} has written a third, and wants you to keep it closed until a day when you need it.

choices.text: Keep it closed

effects.log: You put it in the box with the others. You do not open it. It is enough to know it is there.

choices.text: Write one for {npc} to keep closed too

effects.log: Two closed letters in the box. You both look at them sometimes, and smile, and do not open them.

events.text: {npc} has come home with a pear sapling, a thin whip of a thing with three leaves, for your anniversary. 'Plant it with me,' {he} says. 'Every year we will see if it is still alive.'

choices.text: Plant it in the best spot

effects.log: You dig a deep hole by the south wall and water it every evening. It loses two of its three leaves, and lives.

choices.text: Plant a second one beside it

effects.log: Two thin pear trees, side by side. {npc} says they are for company. They will need it.

events.text: The anniversary pear has flowered for the first time: one cluster of white blossom, very proud. {npc} has invited the neighbours to admire it.

choices.text: Give a speech to the pear

mem.note: made a speech to our pear

effects.log: You thank the pear for its service. The neighbours applaud. The pear drops a petal on {npc}'s head, which is taken as a blessing.

choices.text: Pick the first blossom for {npc}

mem.note: picked me the first pear blossom

effects.log: {npc} scolds you for robbing the tree, and puts the blossom in {his} hair.

events.text: The anniversary pear is a big tree now, heavy with fruit every autumn, and the lane's children climb it. {npc} sits under it with a basket and gives pears away to anyone who passes.

choices.text: Sit under the tree and give pears away too

mem.note: gave away our pears with me

effects.log: You give away a hundred pears. Everybody in the lane knows why the tree was planted. It is a small kind of fame.

choices.text: Plant a new sapling with {npc}

mem.note: planted a new pear with me

effects.log: A new thin whip with three leaves, beside the old tree. 'Every year we will see if it is still alive,' you say. {npc} laughs and takes your arm.

events.text: A cousin of {npc}'s is getting married, and the family tradition is that every couple dances the harvest dance at the wedding. You do not know it. {npc} dances it like falling water.

choices.text: Learn it in secret, every evening

effects.log: You practise behind the shed with a broom for a partner. At the wedding you dance it, nearly right. {npc} stares at you the whole time.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to teach you

effects.log: {npc} teaches you in the kitchen, counting out loud. You step on {his} feet until the pots rattle. At the wedding you only step on them twice.

events.text: Another wedding in the family, and this time you are asked to lead the harvest dance. The family watches.

choices.text: Lead the dance

ok.log: You lead it beautifully. The old ones say they have not seen it danced like that in years. {npc} is pink with pride.

fail.log: You lead it the wrong way round. Everyone follows you anyway. It becomes known as the new harvest dance.

choices.text: Let {npc} lead and follow perfectly

effects.log: You follow so well that nobody watches anyone else. {npc} says afterwards that following is harder, and you let {him} think so.

events.text: At a family wedding, the harvest dance begins, and your knees are no longer what they were. {npc}'s are worse. You look at each other.

choices.text: Dance anyway, slowly

effects.log: You dance it at half speed, the two of you, while the young ones dance it at full. Halfway through, the young ones slow down to match.

choices.text: Teach the dance to the youngest couple

mem.note: taught the dance to the young ones

effects.log: You stand at the side counting out loud, as {npc} once did. The young couple step on each other's feet. It is perfect.

events.text: {npc} is trying to sketch you with charcoal for no reason except that {he} wants to. You must sit still for an hour. You have never sat still for an hour.

choices.text: Sit still, with heroic effort

effects.log: The sketch looks like you with a toothache. {npc} is very pleased with it and pins it to the wall.

choices.text: Sketch {npc} at the same time

effects.log: Two people sketching each other across a table. Both sketches are terrible. Both go on the wall.

events.text: The sketches have become a custom: one a year, each of the other, on the same day. The wall is getting full. You are both getting better, slowly.

choices.text: Sketch {npc} laughing this year

effects.log: It is the hardest thing you have ever tried to draw, and the best. {npc} looks at it a long time.

choices.text: Hang the sketches in a row by year

effects.log: Laid out in order you can see the years on both faces, and the drawing getting better. {npc} says it is the most honest thing in the house.

events.text: A whole wall of sketches, both of you, every year. {npc}'s hand shakes now, and this year's sketch of you is all wobbly lines, and is the best one yet.

choices.text: Tell {npc} it is the best one

mem.note: hung the wobbly sketch in the middle

effects.log: {npc} does not believe you. You hang it in the middle of the wall, where the light is best.

choices.text: Sketch {npc} sketching you

effects.log: You draw {npc} bent over the paper, frowning. {npc} looks at it and says, 'Is that what I look like?' Yes. Always.

events.text: {npc} has lost a jade bracelet, an old one from {his} family, and has turned the house upside down looking. It is not in the house.

choices.text: Search the whole lane

ok.log: You find it in the gutter by the well, where a crow had dropped it. {npc} puts it on and does not take it off for a month.

mem.note: searched the whole lane for me

fail.log: You do not find it. You come home empty-handed and very dirty. {npc} says it does not matter, and is sad for a week.

choices.text: Buy a new one at the jeweller's (12 taels)

effects.log: It is not the same, and {npc} knows it is not the same, and wears it anyway, and holds your hand longer than usual.

events.text: A crow has been leaving things on the window sill: a button, a bead, a scrap of red thread. {npc} thinks it is the crow from the well, paying for something.

choices.text: Leave the crow a bit of meat every day

effects.log: The crow comes every morning and leaves something in exchange. A coin, a pebble, a key nobody can match.

choices.text: Keep the crow's gifts in a box

effects.log: The box fills: buttons, beads, thread, a tiny brass bell. {npc} says it is the best treasure in the house.

events.text: On the window sill one morning is a thin green ring of jade. The crow, very old now, looks at you from the gutter and flies off. It is the bracelet.

choices.text: Give it to {npc}

effects.log: {npc} holds it in both hands and laughs and cries at once. 'Years,' {he} says. 'It kept it for years.'

choices.text: Leave the crow the finest piece of meat in the market

mem.note: paid the crow for my bracelet

effects.log: You leave it on the sill. The crow never comes again. {npc} says it was paid in full.

events.text: {npc} is sure there is something under the bed. Every night, the same announcement, the same small voice, the same request for you to look.

choices.text: Look under the bed with a lamp

effects.log: Dust, a shoe, a lost wooden horse. {npc} is relieved, then suspicious that the thing has hidden.

choices.text: Talk to the thing under the bed
