mem.note: told off the thing under my bed

effects.log: You tell the thing very sternly that this is not its room. {npc} listens, awed, and sleeps well for a week.

events.text: {npc} has decided the thing under the bed is lonely, and wants to leave it a rice cake.

choices.text: Leave the rice cake

effects.log: In the morning the rice cake is gone. The cat looks guilty. {npc} is overjoyed that the thing has eaten.

choices.text: Help {npc} make a bed for it too

effects.log: A little bed of rags under the big bed. {npc} says good night to it every night and stops being afraid.

events.text: Years later, {npc}, grown, tells you the thing under the bed was the best friend {he} had as a small child, and that {he} is leaving rice cakes under a bed for a small one of the neighbours now.

choices.text: Ask if the cat still eats them

mem.note: laughed about the thing with me

effects.log: There is a different cat. It still eats them. Some things are passed down.

choices.text: Tell {npc} you knew it was the cat all along

mem.note: kept the thing under the bed alive

effects.log: {npc} says {he} knew too, and that it did not matter at all.

events.arc: The Frog in the Water Jar
events.text: Your child, {npc}, has brought home a frog and put it in the water jar. {npc} has named it Magistrate, because it looks very serious.

choices.text: Let Magistrate stay, in a separate bowl

effects.log: Magistrate gets a bowl of its own with a stone to sit on. {npc} reports on the frog's moods at every meal.

choices.text: Explain that frogs need ponds

effects.log: {npc} thinks about it very hard, and carries Magistrate back to the pond, and visits every day.

events.arc: The Frog in the Water Jar
events.text: Magistrate has vanished. {npc} is in mourning. Then, in the night, a croak from the garden, where nobody has heard a frog before.

choices.text: Go out with a lamp and look

effects.log: Magistrate is sitting in the rain barrel, very serious. Beside Magistrate sits another frog. {npc} names it Magistrate's Wife.

choices.text: Dig a little pond in the garden

effects.log: It takes a weekend. By summer there are tadpoles in it. {npc} names every one, all Magistrate.

events.arc: The Frog in the Water Jar
events.text: The little pond in the garden is full of frogs now, all descended from Magistrate, according to {npc}, who is nearly grown and still checks on them every evening.

choices.text: Sit by the pond with {npc} at dusk

mem.note: sat by the frog pond with me

effects.log: The frogs sing. {npc} says they are holding court. You both sit until the stars are out.

choices.text: Help {npc} carry the frogs to a bigger pond

effects.log: A procession of buckets to the village pond. {npc} says a short speech for Magistrate's line. The village pond is very loud that summer.

events.arc: The Broken Bowl and the Story
events.text: The rice bowl is broken and your child, {npc}, says a fox came in through the window and broke it. The window is shut. There is rice on {npc}'s sleeve.

choices.text: Ask about the fox, very seriously

mem.note: let me tell the truth myself

effects.log: You ask what colour the fox was, how big, which way it went. The fox gets more and more detailed and then {npc} bursts into tears and tells the truth.

choices.text: Say that a fox is very bad news, and you must tell the neighbours

mem.note: caught me in a fox story

effects.log: {npc} goes pale at the thought of the neighbours, and confesses on the spot.

events.arc: The Broken Bowl and the Story
events.text: {npc} has broken something again, and this time comes straight to you, very red, holding the pieces. 'It was not a fox,' {he} says.

choices.text: Say you are proud of the truth

mem.note: was proud I told the truth

effects.log: {npc} looks astonished. You mend the pot together. It leaks a little, and you keep using it.

choices.text: Make {npc} mend it alone

effects.log: {npc} works at the glue all afternoon. The pot is ugly and whole. {npc} is enormously proud of it.

events.arc: The Broken Bowl and the Story
events.text: {npc}, grown, tells you about a lie {he} nearly told at work, and did not. 'I thought about the fox,' {npc} says.

choices.text: Laugh and tell {npc} about your own fox

mem.note: told me about their own fox

effects.log: You tell {npc} about a lie you told your own elders, long ago. {npc} laughs so hard {he} has to hold the table.

choices.text: Show {npc} the leaking pot, still in use

effects.log: {npc} turns it over in {his} hands, the old ugly glue, and does not say anything for a while.

events.text: Your child, {npc}, has learned to write a few characters at the village school, and has written you a letter. It says: You. Rice. Good. Big dog. It is the best letter you have ever been sent.

choices.text: Write an answer

effects.log: You write back: You. Letter. Good. Big dog where? {npc} reads it, very slowly, and is so pleased {he} writes back at once.

choices.text: Pin it on the wall

effects.log: The letter goes on the wall by the door. Everyone who visits is made to read it. {npc} is mortified and thrilled.

events.text: {npc}'s letters have grown. This one is a whole page, about a quarrel at school, a cricket, a teacher with a terrible cough. There are three characters wrong.

choices.text: Correct the three in red

effects.log: {npc} learns the three. The next letter has none wrong, and is mostly about how there are none wrong.

choices.text: Leave them wrong, and answer the news

effects.log: You answer about the quarrel and the cricket. {npc} learns the right characters on {his} own, a year later, and is outraged that you did not say.

events.text: A letter from {npc}, grown and far away. It is long and grown-up and careful, and at the very end, in large childish characters: You. Rice. Good. Big dog.

choices.text: Write back the same four words

effects.log: You write: You. Letter. Good. Big dog where? The reply comes a month later, with a drawing of a big dog.

choices.text: Send the first letter, taken down from the wall

effects.log: You send the old yellowed page. {npc} writes back that it is on {his} wall now, and that visitors are made to read it.

events.arc: Running Away to the End of the Lane
events.text: Your child, {npc}, has packed a bundle: two rice cakes, a wooden sword and a sock. {npc} is running away, {he} announces, because nobody understands {him}.

choices.text: Ask where {npc} will go

effects.log: {npc} has not thought about that. You discuss it seriously. {npc} decides on the end of the lane, and sets off, and is back by supper.

choices.text: Offer to pack a better bundle

effects.log: You add a blanket, a third rice cake and a lantern. {npc} is moved by this and decides to run away tomorrow instead.

events.arc: Running Away to the End of the Lane
events.text: {npc} is running away again. This time you see the bundle has two rice cakes, and two wooden swords, and {npc} is waiting at the door. 'You can come,' {he} says.

choices.text: Go with {npc} to the end of the lane

effects.log: You sit at the end of the lane with {npc} and eat the rice cakes. It is a very good place to run away to. You are both home by supper.

choices.text: Say you will hold the fort

effects.log: {npc} nods gravely and goes alone. You watch from the window all the way to the end of the lane, where {npc} turns round and waves.

events.arc: Running Away to the End of the Lane
events.text: {npc} is grown and leaving home for real, with a proper pack. At the door {he} hands you a small bundle: two rice cakes, a wooden sword, a sock.

choices.text: Walk with {npc} to the end of the lane

mem.note: walked me to the end of the lane

effects.log: You walk together to the end of the lane. There {npc} turns and waves, and goes on, and you stand there a long time.

choices.text: Hand {npc} a bundle back

mem.note: packed me a bundle for the road

effects.log: Two rice cakes, a blanket and a lantern. {npc} laughs and cries and takes it, and eats the rice cakes before the end of the lane.

events.arc: The Child Who Wanted to Cook
events.text: Your child, {npc}, has been told {he} has a gift for martial arts, and has come to you to say {he} does not want it. {npc} wants to be a cook. {He} is braced for a fight.

choices.text: Tell {npc} to cook

effects.log: {npc} stares at you, then cooks you a dinner that night, nervously. It is very good. {npc} is apprenticed to the inn's cook by spring.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to try both for a year

effects.log: A year of training in the mornings and the inn kitchen in the afternoons. By the end, {npc} has chosen, and you have to admit {he} chose right.

events.arc: The Child Who Wanted to Cook
events.text: {npc} has cooked a banquet for twenty at the inn, on {his} own, for the first time. {He} has saved you the seat by the kitchen door.

choices.text: Eat everything, and say so loudly

effects.log: You praise every dish so loudly that the other diners start to clap. {npc} comes out of the kitchen covered in flour, mortified and glowing.

choices.text: Eat quietly and leave a note

mem.note: left me a note at the banquet

effects.log: Your note says: I was wrong about nothing, and right about one thing. {npc} keeps it in {his} apron for years.

events.arc: The Child Who Wanted to Cook
events.text: {npc} has a kitchen of {his} own now, and a name in the town. On your birthday {he} cooks the first dinner {he} ever made you, exactly, mistakes and all.

choices.text: Eat it all and remember

effects.log: It is not very good. It is the best meal of your life. {npc} watches you finish it with a face you remember from twenty years ago.

choices.text: Cook something for {npc} in return

effects.log: You cook {npc} the one dish you can make. {npc} tastes it and says, very kindly, that you should stick to other things.

events.text: Your small child, {npc}, is burning with fever in the night and will not stop crying. The physician lives across the river and the ferry stops at dark.

choices.text: Carry {npc} across by the shallow ford

ok.log: Waist-deep in cold water in the dark, {npc} held high. The physician opens the door in a nightcap. By dawn the fever has turned.

mem.note: sat up all night with me

fail.log: You slip and soak you both, and come back. You sit up all night with cold cloths instead. By dawn the fever has turned anyway.

choices.text: Sit up all night with cold cloths

mem.note: sat up all night with me

effects.log: Cold cloths, a lullaby you did not know you knew, the long hours. By dawn {npc} is asleep and cool, and you are not.

events.text: {npc} is well and bossy again. You have made a decision: there will never again be a night when you cannot reach the physician.

choices.text: Learn the common remedies from the physician (6 taels)

effects.log: You pay for a season of lessons. Willow bark, ginger, when to worry and when not. You never cross the river at night again.

choices.text: Help the village build a ferry bell

effects.log: A bell on a post by the ferry, to wake the ferryman at night. Three other families use it that winter.

events.text: {npc}, grown, writes that {his} own small one had a fever in the night. {He} sat up with cold cloths and sang a lullaby {he} did not know {he} knew.

choices.text: Write back the rest of the lullaby

effects.log: You write out all the verses. {npc} writes back that the small one is well, and that the third verse works best.

choices.text: Go and visit, with ginger and willow bark

effects.log: You arrive with a bag of remedies and find everybody well and very pleased to see you. {npc} says you are a fever night's worth of help, late.

events.arc: The Kite That Would Not Fly
events.text: Your child, {npc}, has built a kite from a rice-paper sheet and three chopsticks. It is shaped like a dragon, roughly. It will not fly. {npc} is beside {his} kite in the grass in despair.

choices.text: Fix the balance with a tail

effects.log: A long tail of rag strips. The dragon leaps into the air and stays there. {npc} shrieks with joy.

choices.text: Run with it until it flies

effects.log: You run up and down the field for an hour. On the twentieth run it lifts, for a moment. {npc} says that counts.

events.arc: The Kite That Would Not Fly
events.text: {npc} has built a new kite, alone this time, and it flies on the first try. {npc} wants you to fly yours next to it. You do not have one.

choices.text: Build one in an afternoon

mem.note: flew an ugly kite with me

effects.log: Your kite is ugly and flies very badly. {npc} is very kind about it, which is humiliating.

choices.text: Hold the string of {npc}'s kite

effects.log: {npc} lets you hold it. The pull of the string is like something alive. {npc} says you are doing it wrong.

events.arc: The Kite That Would Not Fly
events.text: {npc} is nearly grown and has not flown a kite in years. On a windy spring day you find the old chopstick dragon, its rag tail still on, in the shed.

choices.text: Take it to the field together

mem.note: flew the old dragon with me

effects.log: It still flies, badly. You both run up and down the field for an hour, laughing like idiots.

choices.text: Hang it on the wall

effects.log: The chopstick dragon goes up on the wall. {npc} straightens it every time {he} passes.

events.text: You have given your child, {npc}, a small square of the garden. {npc} has planted everything at once: beans, a melon seed, a peach stone, and one marble, in case.

choices.text: Let it all grow

effects.log: The beans come up, the melon comes up, the peach stone sulks. The marble does nothing. {npc} waters it most of all.

choices.text: Show {npc} how to space the seeds

effects.log: {npc} replants everything properly, except the marble, which stays, for science.

events.text: {npc}'s melon has grown into one great melon, enormous and lopsided. {npc} wants to give it to the oldest person in the lane.

choices.text: Carry it there together

effects.log: The oldest person in the lane is overjoyed, and sends back a peach stone of their own for {npc} to plant.

choices.text: Help {npc} enter it at the harvest fair

mem.note: took my melon to the fair

effects.log: The melon wins nothing; there is a bigger one. But a judge writes on {npc}'s card: Most beloved melon. {npc} keeps the card for years.

events.text: The peach stone from {npc}'s garden, the one that sulked, is a peach tree now, as tall as the wall. {npc}, grown, comes home in summer to pick the first peach.

choices.text: Pick it together

mem.note: shared the first peach with me

effects.log: One perfect peach. You cut it in half. Under the tree, where the plot was, {npc} digs a little and finds the marble.

choices.text: Leave the first peach for the oldest person in the lane

mem.note: took the peach to the lane

effects.log: You carry it there, together, as you once carried a melon. The oldest person in the lane is someone else now, and just as glad.

events.text: Your child, {npc}, has discovered the word why, and uses it on everything. Why is the sky up. Why do dogs not talk. Why do you have to go to work. Why.

choices.text: Answer every why truthfully

effects.log: By the fortieth why you are explaining the movement of the stars and the price of rice. {npc} falls asleep, satisfied, in the middle of the stars.

choices.text: Ask {npc} why back

effects.log: {npc} considers why dogs do not talk and decides they are too polite. This is better than any answer you had.

events.text: {npc}'s whys have got harder. Why do people die. Why are some people poor. Why did the soldier hit the beggar. You do not know all the answers.

choices.text: Say you do not know, honestly

effects.log: {npc} looks at you, surprised, then nods. 'Then we will find out,' {he} says. You find you have no answer to that either.

choices.text: Take {npc} to the temple to ask the old abbot

mem.note: took me to ask the abbot

effects.log: The old abbot listens to all {npc}'s whys and answers one, about the beggar, and gives {npc} a coin to pass on.

events.text: {npc}, nearly grown, asks you a why you have been asking yourself for years, and then, before you can answer, gives you an answer of {his} own.

choices.text: Tell {npc} it is a better answer than yours

effects.log: {npc} pretends not to be pleased, and is. You think about the answer for weeks.

choices.text: Ask {npc} why

effects.log: {npc} laughs, the old laugh from the year of a thousand whys, and explains, at length, until you both fall asleep in your chairs.

events.text: Your child, {npc}, has decided to cook you dinner as a surprise. The surprise is mainly the smoke. There is a fish involved. It is not clear which part of the fish.

choices.text: Eat it and praise it

effects.log: You eat every bite. It is mostly charcoal. {npc} watches you with such pride that you would eat a second fish.

choices.text: Help rescue it

effects.log: You salvage the fish with ginger and rice and a great deal of laughing. {npc} decides it was a team dinner.

events.text: {npc} has been practising, secretly, at a friend's house. Dinner tonight is a fish, cooked properly, with ginger and spring onion. {npc} is trying to look casual.

choices.text: Say it is better than yours

effects.log: It is. {npc} is so pleased {he} drops the spoon. The cat gets the spoon.

choices.text: Ask for the recipe

effects.log: {npc} writes it out with great care. It has a step that says: do not burn it. You keep the recipe in the kitchen drawer.

events.text: {npc}, grown, makes the fish for a family gathering, perfectly, and before serving it, holds a lump of charcoal on a plate in front of you, very solemn.

choices.text: Eat a corner of the charcoal for old times

effects.log: The table erupts. {npc} has to put the fish down to laugh. You chew the charcoal very seriously.

choices.text: Make a speech about the first fish

mem.note: told the story of the first fish

effects.log: You tell the whole table about the smoke and the mystery part of the fish. {npc} hides behind {his} hands and is very happy.

events.text: Your child, {npc}, has been paid for the first time: a string of coppers for a month carrying for the salt merchant. {npc} comes home and puts the whole string on the table in front of you.

choices.text: Accept one copper, and give back the rest

mem.note: took one copper and gave the rest back

effects.log: You take one copper and put it in your sleeve. {npc} looks at you, then at the coppers, and understands something.

choices.text: Help {npc} buy something good with it

mem.note: helped me spend my first wages

effects.log: You go to the market and {npc} buys a pair of good boots, and a sweet for you, which {npc} insists you eat in front of {him}.

events.text: {npc} has been carrying for the salt merchant for a year, and the merchant has offered {him} a place in the counting house. {npc} is not sure {he} is clever enough.

choices.text: Tell {npc} {he} is clever enough

effects.log: {npc} takes the place. The first month is terrible. The second is better. By the third {npc} is correcting the merchant.

choices.text: Teach {npc} to use the abacus at night

effects.log: Evenings at the kitchen table with the abacus. {npc} is faster than you within a month and becomes unbearable about it.

events.text: {npc} comes home with a gift: one copper, threaded on a red cord. 'The first one,' {he} says. 'You gave it back to me, remember. I am returning it.'

choices.text: Wear the copper on its cord

effects.log: You wear it under your shirt. It is warm from {npc}'s pocket and worth less than a bowl of noodles, and you would not sell it for a house.

choices.text: Thread a second copper beside it and give it back

mem.note: added a copper to the cord

effects.log: Two coppers on the cord. {npc} looks at it a long time and puts it on.

events.text: Your mother, {npc}, says {he} does not want any fuss for {his} birthday this year. {He} says it four times, to four different people, loudly, within your hearing.

choices.text: Plan a surprise feast

effects.log: You tell the whole lane, in secret. By the day, the whole lane knows, and so does {npc}, who acts astonished with great skill.

choices.text: Take {npc} at {his} word and make one perfect bowl of noodles

effects.log: Long-life noodles, one unbroken strand. {npc} eats it slowly and says it is exactly the right amount of fuss.

events.text: {npc}'s birthday again, and this year {he} has told nobody anything, which is suspicious. On the day you come home to find a feast laid out, for you.

choices.text: Ask what this is

effects.log: 'You always do it for me,' {npc} says. 'It is my turn to surprise somebody.' The whole lane comes in through the back door, having known for weeks.

choices.text: Eat, and then wash every dish

effects.log: You eat everything and then wash every dish, which is the real gift, says {npc}.

events.text: {npc}'s birthday. {He} is old enough now that the lane makes the fuss without being asked, and {he} sits in the middle of it complaining happily.

choices.text: Make the one strand of noodles again

effects.log: The whole lane watches you pull one unbroken strand. It does not break. {npc} eats it and holds your hand under the table.

choices.text: Give a speech about the four loud no-fusses

mem.note: told the story of no fuss

effects.log: The lane howls. {npc} denies everything, then admits all of it, and says next year {he} wants a bigger fuss.

events.text: {npc} has come to talk about the ox. You were both left half of it, which is a problem, since an ox does not divide. {He} proposes alternate days.

choices.text: Agree to alternate days

effects.log: The ox spends Monday with you and Tuesday with {npc}, and walks between the houses on its own by the end of the month.

choices.text: Let {npc} have the ox outright

effects.log: {npc} protests and then accepts, and from then on lends it to you whenever you need it, before you ask.

events.text: The ox has decided whose ox it is, and it is neither of yours: it has moved itself into the yard of the old widow between your two houses, who feeds it pears.

choices.text: Let the ox stay with the widow

effects.log: The ox ploughs the widow's field, then yours, then {npc}'s. Everyone is happier, and the widow is never short of pears or company.

choices.text: Lead it home with {npc}, one rope each

effects.log: You and {npc} pull. The ox does not move. You both sit down in the road and laugh until the widow brings tea.

events.text: The old ox has died, peacefully, in the widow's yard. {npc} comes to you with the brass bell from its neck, and says it is half yours.

choices.text: Hang it between the two houses

effects.log: You hang the bell on the widow's gate, halfway. When the wind moves it, both of you hear it.

choices.text: Take turns keeping it, a year each

effects.log: The bell goes back and forth every New Year. It is the most important visit of the year, somehow.

events.text: Your grandfather, {npc}, has lost {his} spectacles and has turned the house upside down. They are on top of {his} head.

choices.text: Tell {npc} at once

effects.log: {npc} feels {his} head, finds them, and declares that somebody put them there while {he} was not looking.

choices.text: Help search for a while first

effects.log: You search the whole house together and find a lost coin, a letter and a cat. Then you mention the head. {npc} is delighted with the coin.

events.text: {npc} has lost the spectacles again. This time they are not on {his} head. They are on yours, from when you tried them on yesterday.

choices.text: Confess

effects.log: {npc} laughs so hard {he} has to sit down, and says it is the first time the spectacles were really lost.

choices.text: Find them somewhere clever and return them

mem.note: found my spectacles in the rice jar

effects.log: You 'find' them in the rice jar. {npc} looks at you over them for a long, long time.

events.text: {npc} gives you the spectacles, folded in a cloth. {His} eyes are past helping, {he} says. 'You keep them. You will lose them on your own head one day, and think of me.'

choices.text: Keep them in a box of best things

effects.log: You keep them. Years later you lose them on your own head and laugh out loud in an empty room.

choices.text: Read to {npc} with them on

mem.note: read to me in my spectacles

effects.log: You read aloud through {npc}'s spectacles. They make everything huge. {npc} says that is how {he} always saw the world.

events.text: You and {npc} are having a quarrel so serious that neither of you is speaking. It is the fourth day. Messages are passed through the cat, by talking to it loudly in the other's hearing.

choices.text: Tell the cat you are sorry

effects.log: You tell the cat, loudly, that you were wrong about the thing. {npc} tells the cat that {he} was also wrong. The cat leaves the room.

choices.text: Hold out until the seventh day

effects.log: On the seventh day you both speak at once, the same sentence. You laugh so much you forget what the quarrel was about.

events.text: There is a rule now: no quarrel lasts longer than the cat can stand. Today the cat is ill, and you are both quarrelling about whose turn it is to take it to the animal doctor.

choices.text: Go together

effects.log: You go together, still quarrelling, and stop halfway because the cat looks so miserable. The cat recovers. So do you.

choices.text: Go alone and bring back sweets

mem.note: brought back the cat and sweets

effects.log: You come back with the cat, well, and sweets. {npc} says that is cheating. {He} eats the sweets.

events.text: The old cat of the quarrels has gone, at a great age, and the house is too quiet. You and {npc} catch yourselves talking loudly to an empty cushion.

choices.text: Get a kitten

effects.log: A kitten arrives and sits on the cushion. Within a week it is carrying messages. It is very bad at it.

choices.text: Keep talking to the cushion

effects.log: You tell the cushion, loudly, that you love {npc}. {npc} tells the cushion the same. The cushion says nothing. It is perfect.

events.text: Your child, {npc}, is to sit the county examination for the first time and has not slept for three nights. {npc} sits at the table staring at a book that has not been turned in an hour.

choices.text: Make {npc} go to bed

mem.note: made me sleep before the exam

effects.log: You take the book away and put out the lamp. {npc} sleeps for twelve hours and wakes furious and clear-headed.

choices.text: Test {npc} on the classics till midnight

effects.log: You read questions, {npc} answers. {npc} knows everything. By midnight {npc} has realised it too.

events.text: The results are posted on the county wall. {npc} has not passed. {npc} is standing in front of the wall, very still.

choices.text: Stand beside {npc} and say nothing

mem.note: stood by me at the wall

effects.log: You stand there together until the crowd is gone. On the way home {npc} says, 'Next year.' You say, 'Next year.'

choices.text: Take {npc} for noodles

mem.note: took me for noodles after the wall

effects.log: You eat noodles in the busiest stall in town and talk about everything else. {npc} laughs once, which is enough.

events.text: The county wall again. {npc} is reading the names from the bottom up, too afraid to start at the top. You start at the top.

choices.text: Find the name and say nothing, so {npc} finds it too

mem.note: let me find my own name

effects.log: {npc} reaches the middle of the list and stops, and turns round, and you are already smiling.

choices.text: Shout it

mem.note: shouted my name at the wall

effects.log: You shout the name across the whole crowd. {npc} is mortified and delighted. Strangers clap.
